title: Get your ID
intro: Do these in order. Each one helps you get the next. Rules change by state, so always check the official page before you go.

steps.title: 1. Birth certificate
steps.why: Most other IDs start here.
bring: Your full name as it appears on the birth record
Date and place of birth
Parents' full names (including mother's maiden name)
A photo ID if you have one (if not, ask what else they accept)
Payment (ask if fees can be waived)
A mailing address where you can get mail
tips: Order from the state you were BORN in, not where you live now.
No address? A shelter, case manager, church, or trusted person may let you use theirs. Ask first.
Start from your state's official page. Lookalike sites often charge extra.

links.label: Where to order a birth certificate (CDC, by state)

steps.title: 2. Social Security card
steps.why: Needed for jobs, benefits, and your state ID.
bring: Proof of identity (your birth certificate often works)
The Social Security application form (the SSA site walks you through it)
Ask SSA which documents they accept if you are missing some
tips: A replacement card is free. There are yearly and lifetime limits, so only request one when you need it.
Many people can start online or by phone, then finish at an office.

links.label: Social Security card: how to apply or replace
Find your local Social Security office

steps.title: 3. State ID
steps.why: Your everyday photo ID for banks, jobs, housing, and more.
bring: Birth certificate
Social Security card or proof of your number
Proof of where you live (rules vary; many states accept a letter from a shelter or program, so ask)
Payment (ask about fee waivers)
tips: Check your state DMV site first for the exact document list. It changes by state.
Many states offer a free or reduced-cost ID for people in certain situations. Ask them.

links.label: DMV near me (uses your ZIP above)

title: Mailing address and getting around
intro: No address or ride can block everything else. These are ways to solve both.

steps.title: 1. Get a mailing address
steps.why: IDs, benefits, and bank accounts all mail things to you.
bring: A shelter, program, case manager, or trusted person who agrees to receive mail for you
Or a PO Box (USPS asks for two forms of ID, one with a photo, and a fee)
Or USPS General Delivery: a post office can hold mail for people with no fixed address
tips: Always ask permission before using someone's address.
Call the post office first and ask what they need for General Delivery. Rules vary by location.
If you are leaving an abusive situation, many states have a free confidential address program. The National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233) or 211 can point you to it.

links.label: Find a post office near me

steps.title: 2. Get a bus pass or reduced fare
steps.why: Reliable rides mean you can get to work, appointments, and meetings.
bring: Photo ID if you have one
Proof of income or benefits (for reduced fares)
Ask your program or case manager if they hand out free passes
tips: Many transit agencies have reduced-fare or low-income passes. Ask at their customer service desk.
Treatment programs, job centers, and churches sometimes give out bus passes.

links.label: Reduced-fare transit near me
links.search: reduced fare bus pass low income near

steps.title: 3. Rides to medical appointments
steps.why: Missing a visit because you had no ride is avoidable.
bring: Your Medicaid card or member number
The date, time, and address of the appointment
tips: Medicaid covers non-emergency rides to medical appointments in most cases. This includes treatment and counseling visits.
Call the number on the back of your Medicaid card and ask for non-emergency medical transportation. Book as early as you can.
Your program or clinic can often help set up the ride.

title: Benefits
intro: Food, health coverage, and phone help. Rules and income limits differ by state and change over time, so check your state's official page for the latest.

steps.title: 1. Food help (SNAP)
steps.why: Monthly money for groceries on a card.
bring: Photo ID if you have one
Social Security numbers for people in your household (or proof you applied)
Proof of income, or a note that you have none
Where you live, and a mailing address
Rent and utility costs if you have them
tips: Ask about expedited SNAP. If you have very little money, you may get help within about a week.
Rules about past convictions differ by state. Apply anyway and ask.
Apply through your state's official site or office. It is free.

links.label: Food banks and pantries near me

steps.title: 2. Health coverage (Medicaid)
steps.why: Low-cost or free coverage that, in most states, includes addiction treatment and mental health care.
bring: Photo ID if you have one
Social Security number
Income information (or that you have none)
A mailing address
tips: You can usually apply any time of year. There is no open enrollment window for Medicaid.
Requirements are changing in some states. Check your state's page and ask what applies to you.
If you are in treatment, tell the program. They often help with applications.

steps.title: 3. Phone and internet discount (Lifeline)
steps.why: A federal discount on phone or internet service.
bring: Proof you qualify: you may qualify through SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, or federal housing help, or by income
Photo ID if you have one
tips: Only apply through the official Lifeline site or a provider it lists.
The Affordable Connectivity Program ended in 2024. Ignore ads that still offer it.

title: Bank account
intro: A bank or credit union account makes pay, bills, and getting housing easier.

steps.title: 1. Get your documents ready
steps.why: Most banks ask for the same few things.
bring: Government photo ID (your state ID from the ID list)
Social Security number
Proof of address (a letter from a shelter, program, or lease often works; ask the bank)
A small opening deposit if the account needs one
tips: No address yet? Ask the bank what they accept. Some take a shelter or program letter.

steps.title: 2. Pick an account that won't trap you
steps.why: The right account avoids fees that eat your money.
bring: Ask for a checking account with no overdraft fees and no minimum balance
Ask if they offer a Bank On certified account
tips: Credit unions are often more flexible and cheaper than big banks.
Skip check-cashing stores and prepaid card fees if you can. They add up fast.
If a bank turned you down, ask whether they offer a second-chance account.

links.label: Banks and credit unions near me

steps.title: 3. If you were turned down: check your report
steps.why: Past account problems can show up on a banking report and block new accounts.
bring: Your full name, address, date of birth, and Social Security number to request it
tips: You can get your ChexSystems report free once every 12 months.
If something is wrong, you can dispute it in writing.

title: Phone and internet
intro: Staying reachable matters for jobs, appointments, and benefits.

steps.title: 1. Get a phone plan
steps.why: Employers, offices, and programs need a number to reach you.
bring: Photo ID if you have one
A way to pay, or proof for a discount (see Lifeline in Benefits)
tips: Prepaid plans usually need no credit check and no contract.
Ask about Lifeline before you pay full price.

steps.title: 2. Find internet access
steps.why: Applications, email, and telehealth all need it.
bring: Nothing needed for free options
tips: Public libraries offer free Wi-Fi and computers, often with printing.
Ask internet providers about low-income plans. Many have one.

steps.title: 3. Set up a safe email
steps.why: You will need one for almost every application.
bring: A new email address with a simple, professional name
A password you can remember, written down somewhere safe
tips: Turn on two-step verification if you can.
Never share passwords or codes sent to your phone, even if someone says they are from a bank or agency.
Proton Mail is a privacy-focused option with a free plan. Gmail also works. Either is fine.

title: Phone and account safety
intro: For anyone who thinks someone may be watching their phone or accounts. Read step 1 before you change anything.

steps.title: 1. Read this first: make a safety plan
steps.why: If someone is monitoring you, removing their access can alert them and make things worse.
bring: Use a different device you trust (a friend's phone or a library computer) to look up help
Talk to a trained advocate about a safety plan before removing anything
Think about whether removing access could put you at risk
tips: The National Domestic Violence Hotline is free and confidential: call 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.
If you are in immediate danger, call 911.
Not every worry means someone is watching you. These steps are still worth knowing.

steps.title: 2. Know the warning signs
steps.why: These can point to monitoring, but none of them proves it alone.
bring: Battery draining much faster than normal, or the phone running hot
Data use jumping up for no reason
Apps you do not remember installing
Someone knows things they should not, like where you were or what you wrote
Settings changed that you did not change
tips: Many of these signs have normal causes, like an old battery or an update.
Spyware often hides. A clean look does not guarantee a clean phone.

links.label: Stalkerware: what it is and how to spot it

steps.title: 3. Review apps and permissions
steps.why: This is where unwanted access usually shows up.
bring: Look through your full app list for anything you do not recognize
iPhone: Settings > Privacy & Security > Safety Check (iOS 16 and newer) walks you through sharing and access
iPhone: Settings > General > VPN & Device Management, and look for profiles you do not recognize
Android: look in Settings for Device admin apps, Accessibility, and Install unknown apps. Menu names vary by phone.
Check which apps can use your location, microphone, and camera
Android: run a Google Play Protect scan from the Play Store
tips: Do this after step 1, not before.
If an unknown app has admin or accessibility access, that is a red flag.

steps.title: 4. Check who can get into your accounts
steps.why: Someone does not need your phone if they can sign in to your accounts.
bring: Email (Gmail, Proton, etc.): look at recent sign-ins and connected devices
Apple ID or Google account: look at the list of devices signed in
Social media and banking apps: look at active sessions and logged-in devices
Shared plans, location sharing, and family groups you did not set up
Email forwarding rules or recovery email and phone number you do not recognize
tips: Use a device you trust for this, especially if you think your phone is monitored.
Write down what you find before changing anything.

steps.title: 5. Lock it down
steps.why: Once you are safe to make changes, these close the doors.
bring: Change your passwords from a device you trust, starting with email
Turn on two-step verification, using an authenticator app if you can
Set a new screen lock code that nobody else knows
Update your phone's software
Turn off any location sharing you did not choose
Last resort: a factory reset removes most spyware. Back up only photos and contacts, not apps.
tips: Do this only after step 1, since changes can alert someone who is watching.
A new phone with new accounts is the most reliable fix if you can get one.
